title: DocAnnot - Accelerating the Creation of Key Information Extraction Datasets with GenAI-Powered Auto-Annotation

images.desc:
2.2 Generative AI for Document Annotation


The advent of LLMs and LVLMs has opened up new possibilities for automated data annotation. Recent works have explored using LLMs for data augmentation and knowledge distillation in various NLP tasks. Some approaches have used LLMs to guide the annotation of unlabeled data or to distill reasoning capabilities into smaller KIE models [9, 14]. Among recent efforts, DocKD [14] is, to the best of our knowledge, the only prior work that attempts a similar task. DocKD formulates KIE as a visual question-answering problem, requiring a separate LLM query for each label-value pair, resulting in high computational overhead and use to fine-tune a non-public DocFormerv2 model [4]. In contrast, our approach generates complete KIE annotations for an entire document image in a single LLM call, significantly reducing latency and cost with the novel SCIM algorithm.


Figure 1: The DocAnnot framework for automated KIE dataset generation. Input documents and corresponding data labels are provided to the system. A Large Vision Language Model (LVLM) extracts label-value pairs, while Optical Character Recognition (OCR) extracts text and bounding box information. The Spatially Informed Contextual Matching (SICM) module then integrates these outputs to produce annotated documents, associating text spans with their corresponding labels.

3.2 Automated KIE Dataset Generation: Merging LVLM Insights with OCR with SCIM


For KIE models like LayoutLMv3, UDOP and similar, the training dataset is to be structured such that each document is provided as an image, and an accompanying OCR system extracts a sequence of text segments along with their corresponding bounding boxes. In addition, each text segment is assigned an entity label from a predefined set L={l1,l2,…,lm}L=\{l_{1},l_{2},\ldots,l_{m}\}. Once trained, the model is expected to predict a label for every word it receives as input from the OCR as a token classification problem [7]. This structured format, which comprises the document image, OCR text with bounding boxes, and associated entity labels, forms the basis for our automated annotation framework.


Figure 2: Fine-tuning a KIE model using the output of the DocAnnot framework. Annotated documents from DocAnnot serve as training data for the KIE model fine-tuning pipeline.



3.2.1 LVLM-based Label Value Extraction:


The process begins with a collection of user-provided documents, D={d1,d2,…,dn}D=\{d_{1},d_{2},\ldots,d_{n}\}, and a set of user-defined entity labels L , relevant to the KIE task. An LVLM, denoted as ΦL​V​L​M\Phi_{LVLM}, extracts label-value pairs from these documents. Importantly, for each label, the LVLM outputs not only the corresponding value but also the actual key text as it appears in the document. This can be represented as a mapping:




{label:{actual key text in document:value}}\{\text{label}:\{\text{actual key text in document}:\text{value}\}\}



For instance, a label-value pair may appear as ’sub_total.subtotal_price’:{’SUBTOTAL’:’10,000’}\text{'sub\_total.subtotal\_price'}:\{\text{'SUBTOTAL'}:\text{'10,000'}\}. In this context, the extracted key text (e.g., “SUBTOTAL”) is denoted as tkt_{k} and will be used in subsequent spatial matching.
The overall extraction is expressed as:




L​V=ΦL​V​L​M​(D,L)LV=\Phi_{LVLM}(D,L)



where L​VLV is the set of label-value pairs containing both the value and the key text.




3.2.2 Text and Bounding Box Extraction with OCR:


An OCR engine, denoted as ΦO​C​R\Phi_{OCR}, processes the same set of documents DD. The OCR engine performs:


1. 

Text detection with Bounding Box : Determines the precise spatial coordinates (bounding boxes) for each text segment.



2. 

Text recognition: Recognizes all detected text instances in the document.



The OCR output is represented as:




TB=ΦO​C​R(D)={(t1:b1),(t2:b2),…,(tn:bn)}TB=\Phi_{OCR}(D)=\{(t_{1}:b_{1}),(t_{2}:b_{2}),\ldots,(t_{n}:b_{n})\}



where each bib_{i} corresponds to the bounding box for text segment tit_{i}.




3.2.3 Spatially Informed Contextual Matching (SICM):


The SICM algorithm, denoted as ΦSICM\Phi_{\text{SICM}}, is the core innovation of our framework. Its objective is to reconcile the outputs from the LVLM and OCR modules by assigning the correct labels from LL to the OCR-extracted text segments. Recall that the LVLM produces label-value pairs L​VLV which include the actual key text, and the OCR module outputs a set of text segments with their bounding boxes T​BTB. The SICM algorithm operates in two hierarchical steps:




1. 

Textual Similarity Filtering:
For each label-value pair (li,vi)(l_{i},v_{i}) in L​VLV and every OCR text segment tjt_{j} (with bounding box bjb_{j}) in T​BTB, a textual similarity score is computed:




S​i​m​i​l​a​r​i​t​y​(vi,tj)Similarity(v_{i},t_{j})



using a metric such as the Levenshtein distance. Candidates are then filtered based on this score (e.g., by selecting those exceeding a predefined similarity threshold or by choosing the top-N candidates). Denote this filtered set as T​B′​(vi)⊂T​BTB^{\prime}(v_{i})\subset TB.



2. 

Spatial Disambiguation via Nearest Neighbor:
In scenarios where the same value (e.g., “$3.50”) appears multiple times, textual similarity alone may be insufficient to resolve ambiguity. To address this:


• 

The extracted key text tkt_{k} (e.g., “SUBTOTAL”), accompanied by its bounding box bkb_{k} and obtained during the LVLM stage, serves as a spatial reference.



• 

For each candidate OCR text segment in T​B′​(vi)TB^{\prime}(v_{i}), the Euclidean distance d​(bk,bj)d(b_{k},b_{j}) is computed between its bounding box bjb_{j} and the bounding box of the key text bkb_{k} provided by the LVLM. These distances are used to identify the candidate closest to the key text.



• 

The candidate with the smallest distance to bkb_{k} is then selected:




bj∗=arg⁡minbj∈T​B′​(vi)⁡d​(bk,bj)b_{j^{*}}=\arg\min_{b_{j}\in TB^{\prime}(v_{i})}d(b_{k},b_{j})









To illustrate the disambiguation process using bounding box information, Fig. 3 provides a schematic overview. In this figure, the central element corresponds to the key text (tkt_{k}) extracted by the LVLM along with its bounding box, and the surrounding elements represent candidate OCR text segments with their respective bounding boxes. The lines between them are labeled with the Euclidean distances between the bounding box centers. The line highlighted in red indicates the candidate closest to the key text, which is selected for label-value assignment.


For each label-value pair (li,vi)(l_{i},v_{i}), the label assignment is defined as:




A​s​s​i​g​n​m​e​n​t​(li,vi)=(tj∗,bj∗)Assignment(l_{i},v_{i})=(t_{j^{*}},b_{j^{*}})



meaning that the OCR text segment corresponding to bj∗b_{j^{*}} is selected for label lil_{i}.


Thus, the SICM function is mathematically formulated as:




ΦSICM​(L​V,T​B)={A​s​s​i​g​n​m​e​n​t​(li,vi):li∈L}\Phi_{\text{SICM}}(LV,TB)=\{Assignment(l_{i},v_{i})\;:\;l_{i}\in L\}



and when applied over all label-value pairs, the final annotation is directly obtained as:




A={(tj∗,bj∗,li):li∈L}.A=\{(t_{j^{*}},b_{j^{*}},l_{i})\;:\;l_{i}\in L\}.





This multistage process leverages both textual similarity and spatial reasoning to robustly resolve ambiguities in key-value linking, especially in cases where multiple instances of the same value occur. Such annotated data, combined with the corresponding document images, constitute the training data format expected by state-of-the-art KIE models such as LayoutLMv3, UDOP, and similar models.
